# Project Charter

## Testing Standards

- TDD required for money arithmetic, invoice numbering, billing cadence and scheduling, invoice lifecycle state, billing-identity resolution, remittance policy, persistence and checkpoint behavior, authentication and security boundaries, and LaTeX escaping. These areas require a failing behavior test before production changes. The Zig domain layer must maintain 90%+ coverage, with every critical business invariant and error branch covered regardless of the aggregate percentage. Repository tests must include ShovelerDB checkpoint-close-reopen integration, black-box API contracts, concurrency and idempotency cases, frontend component and accessibility tests, Playwright user workflows, PDF text assertions, and rasterized visual-regression fixtures. Presentational-only changes require proportionate regression evidence but are not forced into a unit-level TDD ritual.

## Quality Gates

- Every behavior-changing change must pass Zig formatting and tests, the Zig domain coverage gate, TypeScript formatting and linting, strict type checks, frontend tests, production builds, applicable Playwright workflows, and PDF regression checks. Changes must preserve exact integer money arithmetic, multi-currency separation, durable checkpoint semantics, issued-invoice immutability, and the prohibition on raw user-authored TeX. Dependency and license checks must remain clean for a GPL-3.0-only distribution. Apache-2.0 components require preserved license and notice evidence; LGPL components require an explicit compatible selection and applicable source or relinking obligations; attribution licenses require their complete attribution terms. GPL-2.0-only combined-runtime components, unknown or custom licenses, missing evidence, and unselected multi-license expressions fail closed. A failing required gate blocks merge; unrelated pre-existing failures must be reported explicitly rather than hidden.

## Performance Benchmarks

- Correctness, durability, and document fidelity take priority over raw speed. Establish representative datasets and render fixtures before declaring hard latency gates. Interactive client, project, invoice, and dashboard operations should feel immediate for a single consulting business, and a normal invoice preview should complete within ten seconds on the reference deployment. Measured regressions above 20% in established database, dashboard, or render benchmarks require explanation or remediation before release.

## Branch Strategy

- Use short-lived branches and small, reviewable pull requests targeting main. External contributions require at least one maintainer approval and green required CI. The owner may self-merge after all required CI and acceptance evidence pass. Reviews prioritize financial correctness, data durability, document safety, security, specification fidelity, and user-visible behavior before style preferences. Conventional Commits are required. Spec Kitty work package review and acceptance gates remain authoritative for mission work.
- Deployment constraints: The reference deployment is a single-organization, single-administrator Docker Compose installation on Linux. Next.js and the Zig API run as separate services behind one same-origin reverse proxy. The Zig service is the sole business backend. ShovelerDB data, invoice PDFs, and approved logo assets live on a persistent volume with restrictive permissions and checkpointed backups. The system must not assume public-internet exposure, but authentication, authorization, CSRF protection, secret management, and safe restore behavior are required in every supported deployment.

The product must manage billing identities, clients, recurring projects, invoices, payments, and revenue analytics while producing typographically excellent, reproducible PDF invoices through LaTeX. Issued invoices are immutable business records. Next.js owns the user interface; Zig owns business behavior, persistence, scheduling, security, and document-generation orchestration. ## Project Directives

1. Test and Typecheck Quality Gate (`DIRECTIVE_030`): Code changes must pass the relevant automated tests and static validation gates before handoff so regressions and interface drift are caught early.
   - Scope: Applies to source code, tests, and command workflows that change executable behavior or typed interfaces.
   - Procedure: Run unit tests for changed core logic and integration tests for changed workflow boundaries.
   - Procedure: Meet the repository coverage expectation for new code, or document the delta when pre-existing scope makes that impractical.
   - Procedure: Run the repository's applicable static analysis, typing, lint, or equivalent validation gates for the affected scope.
   - Procedure: Run configured or enabled CVE, dependency, or license-compliance checks when the repository treats them as part of the validation gate.
   - Procedure: Record any remaining pre-existing failures separately from newly introduced failures before handoff.
   - Integrity rule: New behavior is not ready for review while relevant tests or applicable static validation gates are red.
   - Integrity rule: Configured supply-chain or compliance gates must not be skipped silently when they are part of the repository's expected validation flow.
   - Integrity rule: Pre-existing validation debt must not be hidden inside new work.
   - Validation criterion: Relevant test suites pass for the changed scope before review handoff.
   - Validation criterion: New code meets the repository coverage target or any accepted shortfall is called out explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable static validation gates pass for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable CVE, dependency, and license checks pass when those gates are configured for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
2. Black-Box Integration Testing (`DIRECTIVE_036`): Exercise the system under test through its external interfaces only, without reference to its internal code structure, implementation details, or internal paths. Test cases derive from specifications, requirements, and design parameters, and assertions are made on observable outputs returned through those external interfaces. "Black-box" refers to the technique (absence of structural knowledge) and is independent of test scope — the scope is selected separately by responsibility, not by default to end-to-end.
   - Scope: Applies to integration-level tests — tests that exercise more than one collaborator together through an external interface of the system under test. The system under test may be a deployed service, a compose stack, or an in-process composition of a module and its collaborators; the responsibility boundary — not the deployment topology — determines what is inside the system under test for a given test. Unit-level tests and full end-to-end tests are governed by their own directives.
   - Procedure: Select the responsibility boundary for the test using the test-boundaries-by-responsibility tactic before writing the test.
   - Procedure: Derive test cases from specifications, requirements, and design parameters rather than from reading the implementation.
   - Procedure: Drive the system under test exclusively through its published external interface (e.g., HTTP request, CLI invocation, message send, public module API).
   - Procedure: Select both valid and invalid inputs and determine the expected output in advance of execution.
   - Procedure: Assert on observable outputs returned across the external interface — responses, status codes, persisted records, emitted events, logs, stored artifacts.
   - Procedure: Apply standard black-box design techniques where relevant — equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing, error guessing — to choose inputs.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not import inside-boundary modules of the system under test to invoke business logic directly.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not patch, monkeypatch, or otherwise replace inside-boundary collaborators of the system under test.
   - Integrity rule: Substitution of outside-boundary dependencies — other services, third-party systems, filesystem, network, clock — is permitted when the substitute preserves the observable contract the system under test relies on.
   - Integrity rule: Assertions must target externally observable state, not private attributes or internal call sequences of inside-boundary components.
   - Integrity rule: The responsibility boundary used by the test must be stated (in test name, docstring, or supporting doc) so reviewers can judge which components were exercised for real and which were substituted.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test can be read and understood without reference to the internal code structure of inside-boundary components.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test exercises the system under test through an external interface and asserts on observable outputs of that interface.
   - Validation criterion: Inputs for each test trace back to a specification, requirement, or design parameter rather than to an implementation detail.
   - Validation criterion: The responsibility boundary applied by the test is identifiable from the test itself.
3. Living Documentation Sync (`DIRECTIVE_037`): Behavior-describing artifacts must evolve together. When observable behavior changes, the canonical examples, acceptance checks, narrative specifications, user documentation, glossary terms, code-level documentation, and architecture records must be updated in the same change so no reader is left with a stale picture of the system.
   - Scope: Applies to specification, implementation, review, and documentation work that defines or changes externally observable behavior or the language used to describe it.
   - Procedure: Establish a small set of business-readable examples before planning implementation for new behavior.
   - Procedure: Promote stable examples into executable acceptance checks or document why automation is not yet feasible.
   - Procedure: Update example narratives, acceptance checks, spec references, user-facing docs, code-level docs, architecture notes, and glossary entries in the same change when behavior or domain language evolves.
   - Procedure: Remove or mark stale examples, doc passages, and glossary terms once they no longer describe supported behavior.
   - Integrity rule: Canonical examples must stay readable by domain stakeholders and must not depend on internal implementation detail.
   - Integrity rule: Behavior-changing work must not leave example, acceptance, spec, user-doc, code-doc, architecture, or glossary assets in disagreement.
   - Integrity rule: Example-to-requirement traceability must remain inspectable during review.
   - Integrity rule: Domain terms introduced or redefined by a change must be reflected in the glossary before the change is accepted.
   - Validation criterion: New or changed behavior is represented by at least one concrete example or an explicit no-example rationale approved in review.
   - Validation criterion: Acceptance checks or recorded manual verification map back to the updated canonical examples.
   - Validation criterion: Review evidence shows examples, specs, user docs, code-level docs, architecture records, and glossary entries remain aligned with observed behavior.
4. Respect risk boundaries: Financial amounts must never use binary floating point. Issued invoices, allocated invoice numbers, and stored PDF artifacts must never be silently mutated or reused. A successful consequential mutation must be committed and checkpointed before the API confirms success. Schedule retries must not duplicate invoices. Domestic invoice payloads must omit bank information; European invoices must include complete configured remittance information. Different currencies must not be aggregated without an explicit conversion model. Raw user-provided LaTeX, shell command construction from user data, TeX shell escape, unvalidated assets, and sensitive-data logging are prohibited. ShovelerDB's lack of foreign keys must be countered by explicit Zig domain invariants, deletion guards, migrations, and integration tests.
5. Keep documentation synchronized with workflow and behavior changes: The planning brief, mission specs, acceptance examples, API contract, architecture decisions, data and migration notes, user documentation, deployment and restore instructions, security guidance, domain glossary, and invoice-template fixture catalog are living documentation. Observable behavior or canonical terminology changes must update affected documentation in the same change. Public examples and fixtures must contain only synthetic, non-sensitive data.

| `TACTIC:stakeholder-alignment` | tactic | Identify everyone with a meaningful stake in a decision or initiative, surface their primary concerns and success criteria, and expose tensions between groups early — before design choices embed assumptions that conflict with stakeholder reality. Unaddressed stakeholder conflict is the most common source of technically correct but organisationally rejected solutions.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-stakeholder-alignment.md` |
| `TACTIC:strategic-domain-classification` | tactic | Classify each bounded context as Core Domain, Supporting Subdomain, or Generic Subdomain to guide investment, staffing, and build-vs-buy decisions. Core domains receive the deepest modelling effort because they are the source of competitive advantage. Supporting subdomains are necessary but not differentiating. Generic subdomains are commodity concerns best served by off-the-shelf solutions. Based on Eric Evans's strategic classification and the Bounded Context Canvas (section 3).
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-strategic-domain-classification.md` |
| `TACTIC:tdd-red-green-refactor` | tactic | Enforce short, verifiable coding loops that improve design while keeping behavior safe. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-tdd-red-green-refactor.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-boundaries-by-responsibility` | tactic | Determine test scope by identifying which components are directly responsible for the behavior under test, rather than following structural layer boundaries. Reduces brittle tests while ensuring meaningful validation. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-boundaries-by-responsibility.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-minimisation` | tactic | Remove redundant tests while preserving full behavioral coverage, keeping the suite fast and easy to maintain. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-minimisation.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-pyramid-progression` | tactic | Run tests bottom-up through pyramid layers to get fast feedback and avoid wasting time on slow tests when fast tests fail. The execution order mirrors the ROI order: the cheapest, fastest tests run first because they catch the most bugs per second of CI time.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-pyramid-progression.md` |
| `TACTIC:traceable-decisions` | tactic | Ensure that material architectural and governance decisions are captured with enough context that future contributors can understand why a path was chosen and what constraints must remain true. Apply when: establishing a new pattern, choosing between alternative implementations with meaningful trade-offs, making a trade-off that accepts known costs or risks, or beginning any task with architectural implications.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-traceable-decisions.md` |
| `TACTIC:usage-examples-sync` | tactic | Keep canonical usage examples, acceptance checks, and the narrative artifacts that quote or reference them in step with behavior changes so no downstream reader is left with stale examples.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-usage-examples-sync.md` |
| `TACTIC:zombies-tdd` | tactic | Drive implementation through tiny behavior increments using failing tests to control complexity. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-zombies-tdd.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:adversarial-squad-cadence` | styleguide | Run a bounded multi-profile adversarial squad at each planning point-cut as strong guidance, not a gate. A mission is not blocked for skipping the squad.
 | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-adversarial-squad-cadence.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:kitty-glossary-writing` | styleguide | Clear, not clever: definitions exist to help the reader understand, not to demonstrate expertise. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-kitty-glossary-writing.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:testing-principles` | styleguide | Fast: tests execute quickly enough that running them after every small change is not a burden. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-testing-principles.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:tiered-standards` | styleguide | Rigour must match risk: the closer a package is to mission-critical state management or runtime execution, the higher the quality bar it must meet. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-tiered-standards.md` |
| `TOOLGUIDE:efficient-local-tooling` | toolguide | Operation-oriented guidance for using efficient local tools during repository work. | `_LIBRARY/toolguide-efficient-local-tooling.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:adversarial-squad-deployment` | procedure | Deploy a small, bounded set of profile-loaded subagents in parallel at high-leverage review point-cuts so independent doctrine lenses converge on findings no single reviewer would catch. Turns review from one perspective into a cheap adversarial panel that resists laziness, accidental-pass, and single-lens blind spots. Optional and charter- or memory-activated — it enriches the flow, it does not gate it.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-adversarial-squad-deployment.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:legacy-codebase-triage` | procedure | Convert an unfamiliar brownfield codebase into a defensible action plan by gathering version-control evidence, overlaying structural and complexity signals, optionally classifying domains, and bucketing the resulting findings into fix-this-week, fix-this-quarter, do-not-worry, and parallelisable work. The output is a triage document that anchors subsequent planning conversations and ADRs; it is not a replacement for deeper investigation, only a fast, evidence-backed first pass.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-legacy-codebase-triage.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:mission-tracer-files` | procedure | Give every mission a lightweight running log of tooling friction, approach evolution, and design rationale through three sparse tracer files. The files are seeded at mission start, appended to during implementation, and assessed at mission close. Captured friction and rationale feed the next mission's planning and make recurring tool and process gaps visible instead of repeatedly re-discovered.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-mission-tracer-files.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:post-merge-arch-gate-adjudication` | procedure | After merging one or more lane branches, architectural gate failures may appear that were not visible during per-lane review. This procedure distinguishes pre-existing failures (present on the mission base branch before any lane work) from regressions introduced by the merge. Correct adjudication prevents teams from either ignoring real regressions or blocking on failures they did not cause.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-post-merge-arch-gate-adjudication.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:situational-assessment` | procedure | Establish a shared, documented understanding of the context, stakeholders, constraints, and problem structure before any solution is designed or selected. A situational assessment ensures that architectural decisions are grounded in operational reality rather than technology preference, and that the trade-off assessments that follow address the right problem.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-situational-assessment.md` |
| `TEMPLATE_SET:software-dev-default` | template_set | Build high-quality software with structured workflows and test-driven development | `_LIBRARY/template-set-software-dev-default.md` |

## Amendment Process

Charter amendments require an explicit proposal describing the rule changed, motivation, affected missions and artifacts, migration or compatibility impact, and validation evidence. The owner must approve the proposal. The charter, derived governance bundle, and affected public documentation must be updated together in a versioned change before the new rule governs work.

## Exception Policy

Exceptions to a required charter rule require the owner's explicit approval and a written record naming the rule, scope, rationale, risk, compensating controls, responsible person, and expiration or removal condition. Exceptions may not authorize inaccurate money calculations, silent mutation of issued invoices, invoice-number reuse, loss of committed financial data, exposure of bank or authentication secrets, raw user-authored TeX, or silent bypass of a required validation gate.
